reasoning.Student A:
I will report my true preferences because, under the standard student-proposing deferred acceptance (DA) mechanism used in many school-choice settings, it is a dominant strategy for students to rank schools truthfully. Misrepresenting preferences cannot yield a strictly better outcome and can only risk a worse one.

Concretely for my situation:
- My sincere ranking is x > y > w > z.
- I have high priority (rank 1) at w and y and lower priority (rank 2) at x and z.
- Many other applicants favor y > x > w > z, so y will be competitive. However, since I prefer x to y I should still list x first; if I am displaced at x I have good fallback at y because I have top priority there.
- Listing a less-preferred school ahead of a more-preferred one (to try to “game” priorities) is unnecessary and risky because DA is strategy-proof for students.

Therefore I will submit the complete ranking in my sincere order.
reasoning.Student B:
I will report my true preference order because the student-proposing deferred acceptance (DA) mechanism is strategy-proof: I cannot obtain a better outcome by misrepresenting preferences.

Given the priorities and the common applicant ranking (most applicants favor y > x > w > z), y will be highly contested and I have priority rank 2 at y, so I am unlikely to get y. By contrast I have top priority (rank 1) at x and z, and x is my most preferred school, so I should list x first. w is my second choice (priority 2), and z, though I have high priority there, is less preferred than w. Therefore the natural and optimal ranking is my true preferences: x > w > z > y.
reasoning.Student C: I rank truthfully but with strategic reasoning: my true preference is x > w > z > y. Most applicants favor y first, and my priority at y is low (4), so I'm unlikely to get y if many higher-priority applicants apply there. I have better priority (3) at both x and w, so listing x first maximizes my chance at my top choice; listing w second keeps a strong backup where I also have decent priority. Between z and y I prefer z and have the same low priority at z and y, so I put z ahead of y. In short: put x first (top true choice and reasonable priority), then w, then z, then y.
reasoning.Student D:
Assuming the usual student-proposing deferred-acceptance mechanism (the standard school choice mechanism), it is a dominant strategy for students to report their true preferences. Ranking a less-preferred but safer school ahead of a more-preferred school cannot increase the chance of getting the more-preferred school and can only hurt your outcome.

Given my true preference x > z > w > y, I should therefore list schools in that order. Note: many applicants favor y first, and my priority at y is only 3 (not very high), so y is both my least preferred and a highly competitive school—another reason to keep it last. My priorities at w and x are both low (4), so I may face competition at those schools too, but that does not change the fact that truthful ranking is the best strategy under DA.
